structure.rationale: The requester asked for a small, focused book on what changed between the Java 17/21 world most teams are standing in and the Java 25 LTS they are moving to — six chapters plus a capstone, with a stated omit list (no basics, no JPMS, no GC survey, no Vector/Class-File API, no framework tutorials). The order is the order the features actually build on each other: records give you the data carriers, sealed types plus pattern matching give you the closed domains those carriers live in, virtual threads change how you spend a thread, structured concurrency and scoped values give the virtual-thread world its lifetime and context discipline, the FFM API replaces the last big block of JNI boilerplate, and observability is what tells you whether any of it helped. The capstone then modernizes one small service using every prior chapter, so the reader ends holding a real artifact rather than seven disconnected demos.
structure.audience: Working Java developers who are fluent in Java 8-17 idioms — classes, generics, collections, streams, lambdas, thread pools — and are now targeting Java 21 or Java 25. They do not need an introduction to the language; they need to know precisely what is new, what is final versus preview, and where the sharp edges are in production.
structure.versionPolicy: Every feature in this book is labelled with the JDK version in which it became final, and any feature still in preview on Java 25 is labelled preview at every mention. Java 25 is the baseline; Java 21 is treated as the previous LTS the reader is likely migrating from.

claims.text: Records became a final language feature in Java 16 via JEP 395; they are transparent carriers for immutable data.

A record declaration implicitly creates a private final field per component, a public accessor per component named exactly like the component, a canonical constructor, and implementations of equals, hashCode and toString derived from the components.

Record classes are implicitly final and cannot extend any other class; they may implement interfaces. They cannot declare instance fields beyond the components, but may declare static fields, static and instance methods, and additional constructors that delegate to the canonical one.

A compact constructor declares no parameter list; its body runs before the implicit field assignments, so it is the place to validate arguments and to normalize them by reassigning the parameter variables.

Record equality is component-wise: two records of the same type are equal when every corresponding component is equal, which is what makes records safe as map keys and in assertions where a hand-written DTO would need equals/hashCode maintained by hand.
Records may be declared locally inside a method (local records), which makes them useful as short-lived intermediate tuples inside a stream pipeline or a private algorithm.

A record component of a mutable type (an array, a mutable collection) makes the record shallowly immutable only — the reference cannot be reassigned but the referent can still be mutated, so defensive copying in the compact constructor is required for genuine immutability.

snippets.note: Compact constructor: validate, then normalize by reassigning the parameter. Verified shape against JEP 395.
List.copyOf also rejects null elements and returns an unmodifiable list.

pitfalls: Readers expect a record to be deeply immutable; it is not, if a component is an array or a mutable collection.
Readers try to add an instance field to a record and are surprised it will not compile — the components are the state.
A record is not a shortcut for every small class: if the type's identity matters, or its representation should stay hidden and free to change, an ordinary class is still the right answer.

claims.text: Sealed classes and interfaces became final in Java 17 via JEP 409. A sealed type names its permitted direct subtypes with a permits clause, and every permitted subtype must itself be declared final, sealed, or non-sealed.

The permits clause may be omitted when all permitted subtypes are declared in the same source file; permitted subtypes must be in the same module as the sealed type (or the same package, in the unnamed module).
Pattern matching for switch became final in Java 21 via JEP 441.
Record patterns became final in Java 21 via JEP 440; they deconstruct a record value into its components inside instanceof and switch, and they nest.

A switch over a sealed type whose cases cover every permitted subtype is exhaustive, so no default branch is required; if a new permitted subtype is later added, the switch stops compiling — the compiler reports the gap instead of a default branch silently swallowing it.
A pattern label may carry a guard introduced by the contextual keyword when, e.g. case Circle c when c.radius() > 10 ->.

A pattern-matching switch throws NullPointerException on a null selector unless the switch has an explicit case null label; this preserves the pre-existing behavior of switch while letting new code opt into handling null in one place.
Primitive types in patterns, instanceof and switch remain a preview feature on Java 25 (JEP 507, third preview) and must not be presented as generally available.

snippets.note: Records as the permitted subtypes is the common shape: a closed set of transparent carriers.
Record patterns + a guard, exhaustive over the sealed interface, so no default is needed. Java 21+.

pitfalls: Adding a default branch to a switch over a sealed type throws away the compiler's exhaustiveness check — the single most valuable property of the pattern.
Dominance: a broader pattern placed before a narrower one is a compile error, not a silently dead branch; readers used to if/else chains expect the opposite.
null must be handled with case null, or the switch throws NPE.

claims.text: Virtual threads became final in Java 21 via JEP 444. They are lightweight threads scheduled by the JDK rather than the operating system; a virtual thread runs on a platform 'carrier' thread and unmounts from it when it blocks.

Virtual threads are java.lang.Thread instances, so existing blocking code, debuggers, stack traces and thread dumps keep working — the point of the feature is that blocking code scales, not that code must be rewritten.
The JDK's default virtual-thread scheduler is a ForkJoinPool operating in FIFO mode; its parallelism defaults to the number of available processors.
Virtual threads should not be pooled. They are cheap enough to create one per task; Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() creates a new virtual thread per submitted task.

Because virtual threads are cheap and unbounded by default, a thread pool no longer limits concurrency — a Semaphore is the right way to bound access to a scarce resource such as a database connection pool.
In Java 21 through 23, a virtual thread that blocked inside a synchronized method or block was pinned to its carrier and could not unmount, which could starve the scheduler or deadlock it.

JEP 491, delivered in JDK 24, changed the JVM implementation of synchronized so that monitors are associated with the virtual thread rather than its carrier; a virtual thread can now block inside a synchronized block and still unmount. On Java 24 and later, the advice to replace synchronized with ReentrantLock purely to avoid pinning is obsolete.

Pinning has not disappeared entirely on Java 25: a virtual thread still cannot unmount while executing a native frame — inside a native method or an FFM downcall — or while running a class initializer.
JFR emits a jdk.VirtualThreadPinned event when a virtual thread parks while pinned, which is the supported way to find remaining pinning in a running application.

ThreadLocal still works on virtual threads, but a per-thread copy of a value multiplied by hundreds of thousands of threads is a real memory cost, and thread-local state cannot be shared with subtasks in a disciplined way — this is the motivation for scoped values.

snippets.note: newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor returns an AutoCloseable ExecutorService whose close() awaits termination. Java 21+.
Bound the scarce resource, not the threads.

pitfalls: Teams pool virtual threads out of habit, which reintroduces exactly the queueing they were trying to remove.
Removing the thread pool removes the accidental back-pressure it provided; the connection pool or the downstream service becomes the new bottleneck, sometimes violently.
CPU-bound work does not get faster on virtual threads — the carrier pool is still sized to the CPU count.
Advice written for Java 21 about avoiding synchronized is stale on Java 24+, but advice about native frames is not.

claims.text: Structured concurrency is still a PREVIEW API on Java 25, in its fifth preview via JEP 505; code using it must be compiled and run with --enable-preview and the API may change in a later release.
JEP 505 replaced StructuredTaskScope's public constructors with static factory methods — a scope is now opened with StructuredTaskScope.open(...), not with new StructuredTaskScope<>().

The JDK 25 API expresses the completion policy as a Joiner passed to open(). Joiner.allSuccessfulOrThrow() cancels the scope and makes join() throw if any subtask fails; Joiner.anySuccessfulResultOrThrow() makes join() return the first successful result and throw only if every subtask fails; Joiner.awaitAll() waits for all subtasks without a failure policy; Joiner.allUntil(predicate) waits until the predicate says to stop.
On JDK 25, join() with Joiner.allSuccessfulOrThrow() returns a Stream<Subtask<T>>, so results are read with .map(Subtask::get).

Structured concurrency changed again after Java 25: JEP 525 (sixth preview, JDK 26) makes Joiner.allSuccessfulOrThrow() yield a materialized List<T> in fork order rather than a Stream<Subtask<T>>. Code written against the Java 25 shape will need this one-line change.
A scope is used with try-with-resources: fork() every subtask, then join() once, then read results. Subtask.get() is only valid after join() and only for a subtask that completed successfully.

Scope configuration — a name for observability and a timeout for the whole scope — is supplied through the second argument to open(), e.g. open(joiner, cf -> cf.withName("fetch").withTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2))).

The structural guarantee is that a scope cannot outlive its block: close() waits for every forked subtask, and a failure or timeout cancels the remaining subtasks by interrupting them. A leaked, still-running subtask is not expressible.
Scoped values are FINAL in Java 25 via JEP 506, after several preview rounds. They are an immutable, one-way alternative to ThreadLocal designed for virtual threads.

A scoped value is created with ScopedValue.newInstance(), bound for the dynamic extent of a single call with ScopedValue.where(KEY, value).run(runnable) or .call(callable), and read with KEY.get(). The binding is undone automatically when the call returns, and there is no set() — a scoped value cannot be mutated from inside the extent.
In the finalized Java 25 API, ScopedValue.orElse no longer accepts null as its argument.

Subtasks forked inside a StructuredTaskScope inherit the scoped-value bindings of the scope's owner, so request, tenant and trace context reach every subtask without being threaded through method signatures — this is the pairing that makes both features worth adopting together.

snippets.note: JDK 25 shape. On JDK 26 (JEP 525) join() returns List<Leg> directly and the .map(Subtask::get) drops away.
where(...).run(...) binds for the dynamic extent only; there is no set().

pitfalls: Presenting structured concurrency as generally available on Java 25 — it is preview, and it has already changed shape again in JDK 26.
Calling Subtask.get() before join(), or on a subtask that failed — both throw IllegalStateException.
Reading a scoped value outside its dynamic extent throws NoSuchElementException; use isBound() or orElse when the value is genuinely optional.
Expecting a scoped value to behave like a mutable ThreadLocal — rebinding is done by nesting another where(...).run(...), not by assignment.

claims.text: The Foreign Function & Memory (FFM) API became final in Java 22 via JEP 454, after incubation and preview rounds in Java 17-21. On Java 25 it is a standard part of java.base (java.lang.foreign).
The API has two halves: foreign memory — MemorySegment, Arena, MemoryLayout, VarHandle — and foreign functions — Linker, SymbolLookup, FunctionDescriptor and the MethodHandle a downcall produces.

An Arena controls the lifetime of the memory it allocates. Arena.ofConfined() gives a thread-confined arena that frees everything deterministically when it is closed, which is why it is used with try-with-resources; Arena.ofShared() allows access from multiple threads; Arena.ofAuto() defers freeing to the garbage collector; Arena.global() never frees.

Accessing a memory segment after its arena has been closed throws IllegalStateException, and accessing a confined segment from the wrong thread throws WrongThreadException — the API turns the classic use-after-free segfault into an ordinary Java exception. This spatial and temporal safety is the substantive improvement over JNI and sun.misc.Unsafe.

Linker.nativeLinker() returns the linker for the platform ABI; SymbolLookup.defaultLookup() finds symbols in the libraries the JVM already loaded (libc among them), and a FunctionDescriptor built from ValueLayout constants describes the C signature.
Arena.allocateFrom(String) copies a Java string into off-heap memory as a NUL-terminated UTF-8 C string, which is what a C function expecting a char* needs.

Calling native code is a restricted operation: the module doing it must be named in --enable-native-access, otherwise the JVM prints a warning. JEP 472 is the plan to make this a hard error in a future release, so passing --enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED is the forward-compatible habit.
jextract, which generates Java bindings from C headers, is a separate tool from Project Panama and is not shipped in the JDK.
A virtual thread executing an FFM downcall is in a native frame and therefore cannot unmount from its carrier — long native calls should not be made from unbounded numbers of virtual threads.

snippets.note: The canonical strlen downcall. Run with --enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED. Java 22+ (final).
Use-after-free is an exception, not undefined behavior.

pitfalls: invokeExact is signature-polymorphic: the static types at the call site must match the FunctionDescriptor exactly, or it throws WrongMethodTypeException. Casting the result, as in (long) strlen.invokeExact(...), is part of the signature.
Forgetting --enable-native-access produces a warning today and is planned to become an error.
Reaching for FFM when a pure-Java library exists — the API is safe, but native code still is not.

claims.text: JDK Flight Recorder is built into the JVM and is designed for continuous production use; a recording is started with -XX:StartFlightRecording at launch or attached to a running JVM with jcmd <pid> JFR.start, and dumped with jcmd <pid> JFR.dump.
JFR ships virtual-thread events: jdk.VirtualThreadStart and jdk.VirtualThreadEnd (disabled by default because of their volume), jdk.VirtualThreadPinned, and jdk.VirtualThreadSubmitFailed.

JEP 509 in JDK 25 adds experimental, Linux-only CPU-time profiling to JFR. The new jdk.CPUTimeSample event uses the SIGPROF timer, so samples are attributed to CPU time rather than wall-clock time, and native frames — including FFM downcalls — appear in the profile.

JEP 518 in JDK 25 makes JFR's stack sampling cooperative: stacks are walked at safepoints, which makes sampling safe with ZGC and scalable to concurrent walking. It adds a SafepointLatency event recording how long a thread took to reach a safepoint.

JEP 520 in JDK 25 adds method timing and tracing to JFR via bytecode instrumentation, through two events: jdk.MethodTiming, which records invocation counts and execution times, and jdk.MethodTrace, which records individual invocations with stack traces. Methods are selected by configuration, without changing application code.
JEP 483 in JDK 24 introduced the ahead-of-time cache: classes are loaded and linked during a training run and the result is reused on later starts, reducing startup time.

JEP 514 in JDK 25 simplified the AOT cache workflow from three commands to two: -XX:AOTCacheOutput=app.aot on a training run produces the cache, and -XX:AOTCache=app.aot uses it. The launcher performs the training and cache-creation sub-steps itself.

JEP 515 in JDK 25 stores method execution profiles in the AOT cache, so the JIT can begin generating optimized native code immediately at startup instead of re-profiling — this targets warm-up, not just startup.
Compact object headers shrink the per-object header on 64-bit HotSpot from 12 bytes to 8. They arrived as an experimental feature in JDK 24 (JEP 450) and became a product feature in JDK 25 (JEP 519).

On Java 25 compact object headers are NOT enabled by default: the experimental flag requirement is gone, but the feature must still be switched on with -XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders. JEP 534 proposes enabling it by default in a later release.

Hand-rolled microbenchmarks that time a loop with System.nanoTime are unreliable on the JVM because dead-code elimination, constant folding, on-stack replacement and JIT warm-up all distort the measurement; JMH exists to control for these effects with warmup iterations, forks, and Blackhole consumption of results.

snippets.code:
# Record from launch, using the low-overhead default profile
java -XX:StartFlightRecording=settings=profile,filename=app.jfr,dumponexit=true -jar app.jar

# Or attach to a running JVM
jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=live settings=profile
jcmd <pid> JFR.dump  name=live filename=live.jfr

# JDK 25 AOT cache — two commands (JEP 514)
java -XX:AOTCacheOutput=app.aot -jar app.jar     # training run
java -XX:AOTCache=app.aot       -jar app.jar     # production run

# JDK 25 compact object headers — product feature, opt-in (JEP 519)
java -XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders -jar app.jar

snippets.note: Returning the result lets JMH consume it; a void benchmark needs a Blackhole parameter.

pitfalls: Reporting compact object headers as on by default in Java 25 — they are a product feature but still opt-in.
Reporting JEP 509 CPU-time profiling as generally available — it is experimental and Linux-only.
Enabling jdk.VirtualThreadStart/End in production and drowning the recording in events.
Tuning from a wall-clock profile when the question is CPU cost, or benchmarking without warmup and concluding the wrong thing.

claims.text: A Java 17-era API aggregator typically has four traits worth changing: hand-written DTO classes with equals/hashCode/toString maintained by hand, a fixed platform-thread pool sized by guesswork, outcomes signalled by null or by exceptions, and per-request context passed either as an extra parameter on every method or through a ThreadLocal.

Each of those maps onto exactly one feature in this book: records for the DTOs, a sealed result type plus pattern matching for outcomes, one virtual thread per downstream call instead of a pool, and a scoped value for request context.

A sealed result type makes the failure cases part of the signature: an exhaustive switch over Ok/NotFound/Failed forces the caller to handle each one, whereas a null return or an unchecked exception does not.

The aggregation itself — fan out to N downstream services, fail fast if any is required, apply one deadline to the whole request — is exactly the shape StructuredTaskScope was designed for, but on Java 25 that part of the capstone is preview code and must be built and run with --enable-preview.

A capstone service can be verified with the same JFR recording used in production: jdk.VirtualThreadPinned reveals remaining pinning, jdk.MethodTiming (JDK 25) times the aggregation method without editing it, and the CPU-time profile shows whether the service is actually CPU-bound.

snippets.note: Illustrative before/after; the 'before' body is elided deliberately and labelled as such in the prose.
Exhaustive over the sealed interface — adding a fourth outcome breaks the build, by design.

pitfalls: Modernizing everything at once and being unable to attribute a regression to any single change.
Shipping the preview structured-concurrency path to production without deciding who owns the --enable-preview flag and the JDK 26 API change.
Swapping a thread pool for virtual threads while leaving the downstream connection pool untouched.

volatile: Structured concurrency API shape — preview on Java 25 (JEP 505), changed again in JDK 26 (JEP 525); every StructuredTaskScope snippet in this book needs re-checking against the target JDK.
Compact object headers default — opt-in on Java 25 (JEP 519); JEP 534 proposes enabling by default in a later release.
JFR CPU-time profiling (JEP 509) — experimental and Linux-only on Java 25; status and platform coverage may change.
JNI/native-access restriction — --enable-native-access warns today (JEP 472); planned to become an error in a future release.
Primitive types in patterns (JEP 507) — still preview on Java 25.
JDK version numbers, JEP numbers, and the Java 25 support window.
